paras: The attempted lynching of Charles Burkhart took place in Wenona, Illinois, on November 12, 1888, when townsmen sought to seize and lynch him as the suspected murderer of the banker Peter Howe and his wife. Burkhart cut his throat with a razor as the crowd closed on his rooms, and two later reports described him as a man of mixed race. Papers across the country carried the story under headlines such as "Judge Lynch Cheated" and "Saved the Lynchers Trouble."

Peter Howe, an elderly and wealthy banker, lived with his wife in an isolated house outside Wenona, with Burkhart's stepdaughter Sarah Richardson as their domestic. According to the Ottawa Free Trader, Burkhart came to the house drunk the Saturday before, struggled with the girl, and threatened the couple's lives after they put him out. The New-York Tribune said Howe had ordered him off the premises for trying to collect the girl's wages.

On the morning of November 12 the Howes were found beaten to death in their bed, with a bloody car coupling-pin in the room. The Ottawa Free Trader wrote that the house and grounds soon filled with excited men "demanding the murderer that he might be lynched upon the spot," and that farmers rode to the village, where business stopped and a search began. An Associated Press telegram printed by the Omaha Bee said "a mob of the representative citizens" organized to lynch him and gave him "hot pursuit."

At about nine o'clock, by the Ottawa Free Trader's account, citizens with Marshal Wingate at their head rushed to Burkhart's rooms over a meat market and were met by his wife, who said he was killing himself. The Tribune likewise said he "heard the mob coming" and cut his throat in the hall, where the first man to enter found his body. Meanwhile his stepdaughter was arrested as a possible accomplice, and dispatches warned that she would be lynched if her part were proved.

Sheriff Morrissey arrived from Ottawa with deputies at noon, "apprehensive of difficulty of this kind," after Burkhart was already dead. Coroner Clendennin's first inquest blamed no one, but at a second session Sarah Richardson and Mrs. Burkhart testified that he had confessed the murders to them. The Tribune reported that no evidence implicated the girl, though a Wenona dispatch of November 14 described indignation against her and her mother.

The cemetery association refused a burial permit, and his body went to a Chicago medical college for dissection and was later sold to a Champaign physician. In December the mayor of Wenona helped the widow and her children move to Kansas. No report of any action against the men who pursued Burkhart appears in the coverage.

Only white papers covered the episode, chiefly through a Wenona wire that ran on November 13 in St. Paul, Sacramento, Indianapolis and elsewhere. Headlines treated a lynching as the natural outcome: the St. Paul Globe used "Judge Lynch Cheated," the Waterbury and Wilmington papers "Saved the Lynchers Trouble," and the Macon Beacon "Escapes the Vengeance of the Populace." The Tribune's headline read "Cutting His Own Throat to Escape a Mob."

Closer to home, the Ottawa Free Trader wrote that Burkhart had cheated "the gallows, a fate which he most richly deserved," and the Omaha Bee judged it "well" that he took his own life, since the townsmen would otherwise have killed him. His race entered the coverage only after his death, when the Omaha Bee called him "a mulatto" married to a white woman and an Illinois item said his real name was Lewis and he was "of negro blood."

The widely reprinted Wenona wire described no rush at all, only sentinels posted on his rooms while the county authorities were notified, with citizens saying afterward they would have lynched him. The Tribune telegram and the fuller Ottawa Free Trader account both describe a crowd bursting in, and the AP version calls him "Barnhart" rather than Burkhart.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Charles Burkhart
bases: A crowd of townsmen sought to seize and lynch Charles Burkhart, accused of murdering Peter Howe and his wife, and he cut his throat as they closed in (A1, A8, A12).

Burkhart died by his own hand before the crowd reached him, so no one was killed by the group (A2, A8, A12); the crowd that sought him to lynch him for the Howe murders numbered well over three (A1, A12), but the Ottawa Free Trader puts the village marshal at its head (A12).

Independent dispatches from Wenona, Lasalle, Streator and the Ottawa Free Trader agree that townsmen meant to lynch Burkhart and that he cut his throat before he could be taken (A1, A2, A8, A9, A12), though they differ on whether a crowd actually rushed him or only kept watch (A2, A3).

accounts.label: Wenona wire (sentinels)
accounts.gist: After Irwin suspected Burkhart, a watch of sentinels was placed on his rooms; seeing it, he cut his throat, and citizens said they would have lynched him had he lived.

accounts.label: AP telegram to the Omaha Bee / Streator special
accounts.gist: A mob of citizens organized to lynch Burkhart (called Barnhart), pursued him, and he cut his throat to escape capture; the stepdaughter would be lynched if implicated.

accounts.label: New-York Tribune telegram
accounts.gist: The whole town turned out and rushed his rooms; hearing the mob coming, he cut his throat in the hall and was found dead on the threshold.

accounts.label: Ottawa Free Trader (regional)
accounts.gist: Men at the Howe house demanded the murderer be lynched on the spot; after a search, citizens led by Marshal Wingate rushed his rooms at about nine o'clock and found him dead with a razor in his hand.

framing.detail: The Wenona wire ran as 'JUDGE LYNCH CHEATED' in St. Paul and 'Escapes the Vengeance of the Populace' in Macon, treating a lynching as the expected end without comment on it.
The Bloomington dispatch was headed 'SAVED THE LYNCHERS TROUBLE' in Waterbury and Wilmington.
The New-York Tribune headline read 'CUTTING HIS OWN THROAT TO ESCAPE A MOB' beneath 'WHISKEY AND REVENGE'.

The Ottawa Free Trader said Burkhart had 'cheated the gallows, a fate which he most richly deserved', and the Omaha Bee judged it 'well' that he killed himself, since enraged citizens 'would have made short work of him'.

versions.value: A crowd pursued him or rushed his rooms and he cut his throat as it arrived

conflicts.note: The Ottawa Free Trader, a regional paper with the fullest account, and the independent Tribune telegram both describe a rush on the rooms; the widely reprinted Wenona wire describes only a watch.
Most reports use Burkhart; Barnhart appears only in the AP/Streator version.

Two later reports call him 'a mulatto' and 'of negro blood'; the first-day reports give no race
Never in custody; sought by the crowd and dead before he was taken
Pursuit and a rush on his rooms (contested: the Wenona wire describes a watch only), and threats against his stepdaughter
Townsmen and farmers of Wenona, led by Marshal Wingate in the Ottawa Free Trader account
The domestic was Sarah Richardson, who was arrested; the Ottawa Free Trader adds two inquest sessions at which she and her mother said he confessed

No one was prosecuted for the attempt on Burkhart in the coverage found; his body went to a Chicago medical college after the cemetery association refused a burial permit
